articles.title: Renewable Energy Hits Record High in 2024
content: Global renewable energy capacity grew by an unprecedented 12% in the first half of 2024, marking the largest six-month increase on record. Solar and wind power led the expansion, accounting for over 80% of new capacity.

Experts attribute this growth to falling technology costs, improved energy storage solutions, and stronger government policies worldwide. The International Energy Agency now predicts renewables will surpass coal as the world's largest electricity source by 2026.
articles.author: By Sarah Johnson, Energy Correspondent

articles.title: Electric Vehicle Sales Surge as Prices Drop
content: Global electric vehicle sales reached 15 million in the first quarter of 2024, a 65% increase from the same period last year. This surge comes as battery prices have fallen to record lows, making EVs cost-competitive with traditional vehicles without subsidies.
articles.author: By Emily Wong, Transportation Analyst

articles.title: Green Hydrogen Breakthrough Could Revolutionize Heavy Industry
content: Scientists at MIT have developed a new electrolyzer that produces green hydrogen at 95% efficiency, a significant leap from the current 70-80% standard. The technology uses a novel catalyst that reduces energy requirements while doubling production capacity.
articles.author: By James Wilson, Technology Editor

articles.title: Insect Collapse Threatens Global Food Systems
content: A meta-analysis of 73 long-term studies shows global insect populations have declined 45% since 1970, with climate change now the primary driver in tropical regions. The losses are most severe among pollinators like bees and butterflies that support 75% of food crops.
articles.author: By Kevin O'Brien, Agricultural Scientist

articles.title: Wave and Tidal Energy Projects Gain Momentum
content: Several large-scale wave and tidal energy plants went online in 2024, with projects in Scotland, Canada, and South Korea leading the way. These ocean-based power sources are proving to be reliable, predictable, and capable of powering thousands of homes year-round.
articles.author: By Laura Stevens, Marine Energy Reporter

articles.title: New Battery Technology Doubles Storage Capacity
content: Researchers have unveiled a solid-state battery that can store twice as much energy as current lithium-ion cells while reducing charging time to under 15 minutes. Industry experts say this could be a game-changer for renewable integration and electric vehicles.
articles.author: By Daniel Carter, Technology Correspondent

articles.title: Africa’s Largest Solar Farm Comes Online in Namibia
content: Namibia has launched a 500 MW solar project, now the largest in Africa, capable of supplying clean power to over 1 million households. The project is expected to reduce carbon emissions by 1.2 million tons annually and strengthen regional energy security.
articles.author: By Anita Mensah, Renewable Energy Correspondent

articles.title: AI Optimizes Renewable Energy Grids
content: Artificial intelligence is being used to predict energy demand and optimize the flow of renewable power across national grids, reducing waste and cutting costs. Trials in Germany have already saved millions in operational expenses.
articles.author: By Martin Grey, Energy Systems Analyst

articles.title: Vertical Farming Reduces Urban Carbon Footprints
content: Major cities are adopting vertical farming to grow food locally, reducing transport emissions and water usage. Singapore’s largest vertical farm now produces enough vegetables to feed 200,000 people annually.
articles.author: By Olivia Chen, Sustainability Writer

articles.title: Recycling Wind Turbine Blades Becomes Viable
content: New chemical recycling methods are allowing old wind turbine blades to be turned into materials for bridges, playgrounds, and even new turbines, solving a long-standing waste problem in the wind industry.
articles.author: By Laura Bennett, Environmental Technology Journalist

articles.title: Solar Desalination Plants Transform Water Access
content: Coastal communities in drought-prone areas are adopting solar-powered desalination plants to provide fresh water sustainably, with projects in Morocco and Australia showing great promise.
articles.author: By Ahmed Karim, Climate Solutions Reporter
